crosscheck_source: Pearson GSE Grammar for adult learners 2023
crosscheck_policy: GSE Grammar is supporting/cross-check evidence mapped to reviewed grammar supercategories; it does not create a second independent target inventory.
grammar_family_stage_policy: Only lifecycle stages explicitly present in the reviewed grammar-family source are copied; missing early-level stages are not invented.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘that’ and ‘this’ as determiners relating to people or objects.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I like this film. Can you see that woman?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present continuous to refer to events at the time of speaking.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: present continuous for time of speaking
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m watching TV. What are you doing? She’s not listening. He’s checking his email.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask about quantities using ‘how much/ many’ with count and uncountable nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: Questions with ‘how much/many’ + count/ mass nouns
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How much do you earn? How many children do they have?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Verb | Tags and question forms Noun | Mass/count

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make affirmative statements using common irregular past simple forms.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: irregular past simple for finished time (affirmative only)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We saw the match. They went to London.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘and’ with verbs and verb phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We eat and (we) sleep in the hotel. She’s an IT expert, and she speaks good English.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask yes/no questions using the past tense of verbs.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Did you see him? Did they catch their plane?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘s’’ to express possession with plural nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the soldiers’ guns the students’ books

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘at’ as a preposition of time.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: at two o’clock at lunchtime at the weekend

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use an adjective as a subject complement after a linking verb.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Chiara is Italian. You look tired.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adjective | Position Clause | Basic construction Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make affirmative statements using common regular past simple forms.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: regular past simple for finished time (affirmative only)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I asked a question. They walked home.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of prepositions of place.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: against; behind; in front of; next to; under

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘like/hate/love’ with the ‘-ing’ forms of verbs.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I love going to museums. Do you like working here? She hates watching TV. They love dancing.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask for information about time, measurement, size etc. with ‘how’ + adjective/quantifier.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘how’ questions for time, measurement, size etc. (except ‘much/many’)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How big is it? How tall is he? How long is the film?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Verb | Tags and question forms Pronoun | Question words

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can place adjectives in the correct position (before nouns).
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a white car a small box of biscuits

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common time expressions with ‘past’/’to’ and fractions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a quarter to/past three half past six

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘want to’ + infinitive to express intentions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I want to help you. Do they want to buy it?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask wh- questions using the past tense of verbs.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Where did you go? How much did it cost? When did he arrive?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Verb | Tags and question forms Pronoun | Question words

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘after’ as a preposition in time expressions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: after the show after dinner

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use uncountable (mass) nouns with no quantifier or an appropriate quantifier.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I want some food, She doesn’t eat cheese. Do we have any paper?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Determiner | Articles Noun | Mass/count

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘was’ and ‘were’ with a range of complement phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It was cold yesterday. He wasn’t at school last week. We were in Mexico on Monday.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Basic construction Verb | Tense Clause | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can link clauses and sentences with a range of basic connectors.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I did the shopping and cleaned the house. It’s the right size, but I don’t like the colour. We can get the bus, or go there by train.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the definite article to refer to a specific person, thing, or situation.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the hotel manager the British people the house on the hill

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form questions with ‘How often’ in the present tense.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How often do you go to the beach? How often does it rain?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Quantifiers Verb | Tags and question forms Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘this’ with time expressions referring to the present or future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: this week this Monday this weekend this lesson this afternoon

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can give, deny or ask about permission in the present and near future with ‘can’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Can I have some more? You can’t use a phone in class. He can’t take my car I need it.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘can’t’ to decline offers and invitations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Sorry, I can’t come on Friday. I’m afraid I can’t eat that.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Modal verb | Ability

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask questions about how to do things.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: How do you get there? How do you do it?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common adverbs of frequency.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It always rains. She never smokes. They usually come by car.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adverb | Time Adverb | Position Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make requests and offers with ‘would like’ + nouns and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’d like some more soup. Would you like a cup of tea?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Clause | Conditional

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make basic polite requests with ‘could’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Could I have a drink? Could you repeat that?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the correct preposition (‘on’ or ‘at’) with various common time expressions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: On Friday at 7 p.m. at the same time as …

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can describe times exactly using numbers from 1 to 59 (+ ‘past/to’).
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: exact time expressions with numbers from 1 to 59 (plus ‘past/to’)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: five seventeen sixteen minutes to seven one minute past three

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘it’ as a dummy (impersonal) subject when talking about weather conditions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s raining. It’s very windy tonight.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘(not) here’ and ‘(not) there’ to refer to presence and absence.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s plenty of food here. There’s no one there.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make offers, requests, and suggestions using ‘can’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Can I help you? Can we meet for a coffee? Can you tell her you’re sorry?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Modal verb | Obligation

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form questions with ‘what’ and ‘which’ as adjectives.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What temperature is it? Which train did he get?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Question words Pronoun | Question words Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form questions with ‘whose’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Whose is this? Whose car is that?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Possessive Pronoun | Question words Determiner | Question words

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘can’ and ‘can’t’ with verbs of perception.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I can see you. We can’t hear him.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘Let’s …’ for suggestions and invitations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Let’s go to a movie. Let’s have dinner now.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common adverbs of movement and direction.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: going back coming down turn left/right travelling west

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common time markers for the past, present and future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: time markers for past, present and future
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: ago last night/week yesterday right now at the moment next Saturday/week
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adverb | Time Clause | Time Preposition | Time

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express personal plans and intentions for the future using ‘going to’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m going to change my job. Susan’s going to call a meeting.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make requests and offers with ‘would like to’ + verbs in the infinitive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’d like to go home. Would you like to borrow some money?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Wishes and intentions Clause | Conditional Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘(not) many/much’ with count (countable) and mass (uncountable) nouns respectively.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Many people live there. There isn’t much food in my apartment.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the definite article to refer back to something already mentioned.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She was in the meeting too. Did you see the match last night?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use plural countable nouns without an article or quantifier.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: zero (dummy) quantifier with plural countable nouns
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I love dogs. Cars are expensive.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘because’ with verb phrases to refer to causes and reasons.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I can’t buy it because I haven’t got any money. Because she loves you, she forgives you.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Cause and result Clause | Result/cause

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common prepositions of movement.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: get on/off the bus get into/out of bed walk/go to work jump into the water

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘please’ in the correct position with imperative verb forms.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Please don’t say anything. Come here, please.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘will’ to ask questions about the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Will you be here tomorrow? Will she come back?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tags and question forms Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form the superlative of longer regular adjectives with ‘most’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the most expensive the most interesting

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use uncountable nouns without an article.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We need food. There’s no gas.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘a lot of/lots of’ to refer to quantities.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a lot of money lots of people

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘should(n’t)’ to offer or ask for advice or suggestions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You should go to a doctor. He shouldn’t drink so much. Where should we go?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make comparisons with ‘more’ + longer adjectives.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You’re more intelligent than me. The film was more interesting than the book.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use adverbs of frequency and manner in the correct position.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: position of adverbs of frequency and manner
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I never watch TV. She drives that car very fast. You should always tell the truth. He’s always late.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adverb | Position Adverb | Time Clause | Basic construction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form the superlative of regular adjectives with ‘-est’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the biggest the funniest

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘of’ to refer to possession and attribution.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the property of the school; the colour of her hair; the start of the lesson

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can correctly place adverbs of frequency in longer sentences.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: position of adverbs of frequency (before/ after verb)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She ^ goes to work by car. (always) I have ^ eaten in this restaurant. (often)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask questions with ‘what kind/sort of …?’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What kind of cheese is this? What sort of music do you like?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Question words Pronoun | Question words Preposition | Logical

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can deny intention and desire with ‘wouldn’t like/don’t want to …’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I wouldn’t like to live here. I don’t want to eat that.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Wishes and intentions Clause | Conditional Verb | Auxiliary

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can correctly use a range of nouns with both countable and uncountable meanings.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: This coffee is too hot. I want three coffees. I really love cheese. She bought three cheeses.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘some’ as a quantifier with count and mass nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘some’ in affirmative statements with countable and uncountable nouns
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s some milk in the fridge. Some men are waiting outside.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘with’ and ‘without’ to refer to (lack of) possession and attribution.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a boy with dark hair a car with a sunroof the woman with a child a computer without a screen

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express obligation and necessity in the present and near future with ‘have to’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘have to’ for present and near future obligation
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I have to do my homework. I have to get up early tomorrow. You don’t have to pay.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form basic adverbs by adding ‘-ly’ to adjectives.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Slowly, badly, carefully

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of basic quantifiers with ‘of’ and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Lots of people like him. I lost some of my money. We’ve had a bit of luck.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘must’ to express obligation and necessity in the present and near future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You must try to relax. I must cook dinner now. Must you go?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can generalise about persons, things, or situations using plural nouns/noun phrases with no (zero) article.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: People are kind. I don’t like dogs.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use verb + ‘-ing’ forms as the complement of a sentence.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I love watching football. I hate studying English. She enjoys swimming in the sea.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form and use irregular adverbs.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: good – well fast – fast hard - hard

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use phrases with prepositions + adjectives + nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: a woman with an old hat and a cheap coat two men in a large black car

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘some’ and ‘any’ as quantifiers in negative statements and questions with mass and count nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘some’ and ‘any’ in questions and negative statements with countable and uncountable nouns
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Can I have some coffee? Do you want some chocolate/biscuits? Is there any bread? There aren’t any biscuits left.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common adverbs and adverbial phrases of position.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the level above sitting at the back the man in the middle

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘will’ + infinitive for predictions about the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: That will be really difficult. She’ll be late. I’m sure it won’t be open.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Time-related Verb | Auxiliary Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express means using ‘by’ with nouns and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘by’ + NP for means of doing something
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: go by bus/train/bike send it by email

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can distinguish between adjectives ending with ‘-ed’ and ‘-ing’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m bored. It’s a very boring film. We’re very excited. It was an exciting party.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form irregular superlatives of adjectives and adverbs such as ‘best’, ‘worst’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the best the worst
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adjective | Comparison Clause | Comparison Adverb | Comparison

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make comparisons with regular shorter adjectives + ‘-er’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The journey by road is quicker (than by train). She’s cleverer than me.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present continuous to refer to temporary situations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m staying with my parents. She’s working in Oxford. She’s working a lot at the moment.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘in’ as a preposition of time with future reference.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: in four weeks in a few minutes

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘so’ to refer to results and consequences.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s raining, so we’re staying in. He failed the exam, so he didn’t get the certificate.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Cause and result Clause | Result/cause

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask wh- questions about the subject.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Who loves you? Who saw you? What eats birds? Who is sitting here?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Question words Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ’ll+ infinitive for spontaneous decisions and offers.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’ll get it. We’ll help you.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make statements and questions with ‘know’ + wh-clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I know where he lives. Do you know what they want?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Reported speech and ideas Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘no’ as a quantifier to indicate the absence or lack of something.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s no sugar left. There are no chocolates in this box. There’s no time to do it.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express sufficiency and insufficiency with ‘enough’ and ‘too’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We have enough bread. There are too many people here. Don’t have enough money.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use adjectives after verbs of sensation (e.g. ‘look, sound, feel, taste, smell, seem, appear’).
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She looks tired. It smells nice.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘that’ and ‘this’ as subject and object pronouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: That’s clear This is ridiculous Have a look at this.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use direct + indirect objects together after ditransitive verbs like ‘give/tell/pass’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: usage of common ditransitive verbs such as ‘give/tell/pass’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Pass her the book. Give it to him. Give them some food. Don’t tell me lies.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Basic construction Pronoun | Personal Verb | Imperative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make irregular comparisons of adjectives and adverbs such as ‘better’, ‘worse’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: inflected comparative forms of irregular adjectives and adverbs
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s better here than in London. I’m feeling worse today.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adjective | Comparison Adverb | Comparison Clause | Comparison

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the definite article correctly with geographical names and locations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: definite article for: uniqueness, public buildings, geographical names, other proper names
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the Black Sea the White House

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘before/after’ as conjunctions with complement clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: after we got home before she had finished speaking

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can distinguish between the past simple and past continuous.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I opened the door when you arrived. vs I was opening the door when you arrived.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make statements with the verb ‘be’ and adjectives with verbs in the infinitive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It was good to see you. It’s difficult to pass the exam. It wasn’t easy to find the restaurant.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use all forms of comparatives and superlatives of adjectives.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: the best news older than him the most useful present speaking more slowly

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use singular verb forms with impersonal pronouns ‘every/any/no/ some+body/where/one/thing’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: No one is safe. Everything looks good.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘May I/we ...?’ for formal and polite requests for permission.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: May we come in? May I explain what I mean?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘when’ to link two clauses in the past simple.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I met him when I was at school. I played tennis when I was young.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Time Verb | Tense Clause | Time

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘so …’ to express results and consequences.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You weren’t there, so I came home. He was very tired, so he went to bed early.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can distinguish between the most common ways of expressing the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: comparison of all common future forms (‘going to’, ‘will’, present simple and present continuous)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’m going to go to bed now. vs. I’ll go to bed later. The train leaves at 2:15. vs. I’m leaving for Spain in two weeks.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present perfect to refer to personal experiences in the past.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: present perfect for personal experiences in the past
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She’s worked in several countries. I’ve been to Kiev before. Have you seen Star Wars?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of indefinite compound pronouns prefixed with ‘some-’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Someone is waiting for you. I need something to eat.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can refer to impossibility and inability in the past using ‘couldn’t’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I couldn’t go to the party. I couldn’t swim when I was ten. Women couldn’t vote in the 19th century.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can qualify adverbs with ‘really/quite/very’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He talks really fast. She goes there quite often. She can speak Chinese very well.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask questions using the present perfect with ‘ever’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Have you ever been to Las Vegas? Has she ever seen your apartment?

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘a bit/a little’ to refer to quantities with mass (uncountable) nouns.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s only a little/a bit of milk left. There’s a little/a bit of money in the desk.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make offers and suggestions using ‘could’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I could drive you to the airport. You could look it up on the internet.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Requests, offers and permission Modal verb | Obligation

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘like’ with sensory verbs to express similarity.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She looks like her mother. It tastes like chocolate.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present perfect with present reference.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: present perfect with present reference (indefinite past)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’ve hurt my knee. He’s cooked us a delicious dinner.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can report current and future plans and intentions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He says he can do it. She tells me she’s happy

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the present continuous with future reference.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What are you doing on Saturday? We’re playing tennis tomorrow. We’re meeting at 3 p.m.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘both’ and ‘both of’ with nouns and noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: They both went home. I want both of them.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Determiner | Conjunction and disjunction Conjunction | Coordinating Adverb | Conjunction and disjunction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of pronouns and adverbials for anaphoric (back) reference.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The child was unhappy; he wanted his mother. I quickly walked home. There I found Marsha waiting for me. The house had already been sold. This was a great surprise to me.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can construct double-complement sentences with verbs such as ‘give’, ‘tell’, ‘ask’, etc.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: give him the book tell me the time ask them a question

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express basic cause and effect with ‘because of …’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We didn’t go out, because of the weather. Because of my illness, I wasn’t able to go with them.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Preposition | Logical Preposition | Cause and result Clause | Result/cause

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can form adjectives from nouns with common affixes.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: adjectives from nouns with common suffixes (‘-y’, ‘-ful’)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: success - successful sport - sporty
